sections.p00.s0: One-time installation and configuration. Do the steps in order in one sitting (about 1 to 2 hours), and open a fresh terminal after each install so PATH changes take effect. Everything later in the course assumes these commands work.
sections.p00.s1: The Git model and commands you will use every day. Read each topic, then try it in a throwaway repository straight away. Spend most time on the index/HEAD model (s1.1) and on revert/reset/rebase (s1.5); the rest follows from those.
sections.p00.s2: A drill in one repository that exercises everything from Learn. Do the steps in order in the same git-training repo, running git status and git log --oneline --graph --all after each one. Repeat the whole drill from scratch until it takes under 30 minutes.

p00.s0.0.how: Install from python.org (on Windows tick 'Add python.exe to PATH', or use the py launcher). Close all terminals, open a new one and run python --version and py -0 to list installed versions.
p00.s0.0.done: A new terminal prints Python 3.13 or later for python --version.

p00.s0.1.how: Install uv with the standalone installer from its docs, open a new terminal, run the command, then list the scratch folder: note pyproject.toml, main.py and the .venv created by uv run.
p00.s0.1.done: The command prints 1, and you can say what pyproject.toml and .venv are for.

p00.s0.2.how: Install VS Code, add the Python extension (Pylance comes with it), open the scratch folder and choose its .venv interpreter with 'Python: Select Interpreter'. Run main.py with F5.
p00.s0.2.done: The status bar shows the .venv interpreter and F5 runs the file with the debugger.

p00.s0.3.how: Create the account, run ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com", add the public key (.pub file) in GitHub settings, then run ssh -T git@github.com.

where.name: GitHub: Generating a new SSH key

p00.s0.3.done: ssh -T git@github.com greets you by your GitHub username.

p00.s0.4.how: Set both values, using the email on your GitHub account (or GitHub's noreply address) so commits link to your profile. Check with git config --global --list.
p00.s0.4.done: git config user.name and git config user.email print the values you set.

p00.s0.5.how: Run the command (needs Git 2.28 or later; check with git --version), then run git init in an empty folder and git status.
p00.s0.5.done: git status in a new repository reports 'On branch main'.

p00.s1.0.how: Read how Git stores data, then in a test repo run git cat-file -p HEAD and follow the tree hash with git cat-file -p to see the full file listing stored in one commit.
p00.s1.0.done: You can explain why git diff output is computed from two snapshots rather than stored.

p00.s1.1.how: Read the three trees section. Edit a file, then compare git diff, git diff --staged and git status before and after git add. Run git remote -v in a cloned repo to see origin.
p00.s1.1.done: You can draw working tree, index, HEAD and origin and say which command moves changes between each pair.

p00.s1.2.how: In a new repo run each command in the order listed, with git status between them. Make three commits, then read them with git log --oneline and git log -p.

where.name: Pro Git: Viewing the commit history

p00.s1.2.done: From memory you can create a repo, make a commit and show what changed in it.

p00.s1.3.how: Create a branch with git switch -c, commit on it and on main to the same line of one file, then git merge. Edit out the conflict markers by hand, git add the file and commit.

where.name: Pro Git: Basic branching and merging
Pro Git: Branches in a nutshell

p00.s1.3.done: You resolved a conflict without a GUI and git log --graph shows the merge commit.

p00.s1.4.how: Push a repo to GitHub, edit a file on the GitHub website, then compare git fetch plus git log origin/main with git pull. Discard a local edit with git restore and park one with git stash.
p00.s1.4.done: You can say the difference between fetch and pull, and between restore and stash.

p00.s1.5.how: Read Reset Demystified and the Rebasing chapter, including 'The Perils of Rebasing'. In a test repo undo one commit with git revert, then with git reset --soft HEAD~1, and compare git log.
p00.s1.5.done: You can explain why revert is safe on pushed commits and reset and rebase are not.

p00.s1.6.how: Complete the Introduction to GitHub course. Then open a pull request against your own repo from a branch, leave line comments on the diff, and merge it.
p00.s1.6.done: You have a merged pull request with at least one review comment on a changed line.

p00.s2.0.how: Run git init git-training, write a short README.md and an app.py that prints a greeting, and commit them as two separate commits with clear messages.

where.name: Pro Git: Getting a Git repository

p00.s2.0.done: git log --oneline shows two commits and git status is clean.

p00.s2.1.how: Run git switch -c feature/calculator, add an add(a, b) function to app.py, commit, then switch back to main and confirm the function is absent there.

where.name: Pro Git: Basic branching and merging

p00.s2.1.done: git log --oneline --all --graph shows the feature branch one commit ahead of main.

p00.s2.2.how: On main, edit the same lines of app.py differently and commit. Run git merge feature/calculator, resolve the markers by hand, run python app.py, then git add and commit.

where.name: Pro Git: Basic branching and merging

p00.s2.2.done: The merge commit exists, app.py has no conflict markers, and the program runs.

p00.s2.3.how: Edit app.py without committing, run git stash, switch to the other branch and back, then git stash pop. Check git stash list before and after.
p00.s2.3.done: Your uncommitted edit reappears after pop and git stash list is empty.

p00.s2.4.how: On the feature branch run git reset --hard HEAD~1, or delete the branch with git branch -D. Find the lost commit in git reflog and restore it with git reset --hard or git branch and its hash.
p00.s2.4.done: The branch points at the lost commit again and you can do the recovery without notes.
